name: separated-interface
intent: Declare the contract in a deployment unit of its own so that clients depend only on the interface while the implementation lives - and can be deployed - somewhere else.
problem: A dependency or deployment rule forbids the client package from depending on the package that holds the implementation, yet the client must call the implementation's operations. Keeping the interface next to the implementation drags the implementation's own dependencies into the client's dependency graph, and a client that cannot ship or load the implementation (embedded target, plugin host, published header set, ABI boundary) cannot use it at all.
context: Systems partitioned into packages, assemblies, modules, crates or shared libraries with enforced dependency direction: layered and hexagonal architectures, plugin and driver hosts, library ABI firewalls, multi-platform products, and test setups where a fake must stand in for the real component. Applies when contract and implementation can be carried by separate units, or when the contract must be usable where the implementation cannot go.
benefits: Dependency direction is controlled: the client unit depends only on the contract unit, so the implementation's dependencies, platform requirements and licence never enter the client's dependency graph.
Deployment separation: the contract can ship to code that cannot carry the implementation - an embedded or device client, a plugin host, a published header set, a native add-on or remote boundary.
Implementations become substitutable: a second implementation (test fake, per-platform, per-vendor, per-tenant) is bound at the composition root without touching client code.
Dependency cycles disappear: two units that need each other's operations can both depend on the contract unit instead of on each other.
Testing improves: fakes implement the contract directly, so unit tests run without the real infrastructure.
Third parties can extend the system through a documented contract without modifying or recompiling the host (plugin points, service provider interfaces).
tradeoffs: Indirection with a runtime failure mode: clients no longer construct what they use, so a missing registration, provider or module is discovered when the wiring runs - not by the compiler.
Contract evolution is the hard part: once third parties implement the interface, adding a member breaks them; changes need default methods, optional capabilities or a new versioned interface.
Over-abstraction: an interface with one implementation and one consumer adds a type, a file and often a deployment unit while buying no substitutability and no deployment boundary.
Version skew between contract and implementation artifacts must be managed explicitly (ABI/SPI compatibility, classpath and module-path resolution).
Discoverability drops: nothing in the client names the running type, so wiring conventions, registries or service files are needed to answer which implementation is live.
In dynamic languages the contract is unenforced at runtime; a collaborator that almost satisfies it fails at the call, not at the boundary.

participants.responsibility: Declares the operations and their semantics in terms of the client's needs; carries no implementation and as few dependencies as possible so it can be deployed anywhere.
Depends only on the interface; never names, imports or constructs a concrete implementation.
Realises the contract in its own deployment unit; is invisible to the client at compile time and often at runtime.
The package, module, crate, assembly or header set that carries the interface - the only artifact both sides are allowed to depend on.
The one place that knows both sides: a factory, DI container, service loader or registry binds an implementation to the contract at start-up.

use_cases: Hexagonal / ports-and-adapters architectures: the domain declares ports (repository, clock, notifier) in its own package and infrastructure supplies the adapters.

Plugin hosts, drivers and service provider interfaces: the host ships only the contract; providers are deployed later and discovered through module descriptors, service loader files, registries or configuration.

Library ABI boundaries: clients compile against a header or protocol definition while the implementation stays inside a shared library (C opaque handles, C++ pure abstract classes or pimpl, framework bundles).
Multi-platform products: one contract with per-platform implementations selected at build or run time.
Test doubles: fakes or in-memory implementations of the contract are injected in tests while production wiring binds the real component.
Remote or deferred work: the local interface is implemented by a stub, proxy or gateway that forwards across a process or network boundary (the plug point Fowler names for Gateway).

JDBC: applications compile only against java.sql (Driver, Connection) in the JDK's own contract module; the vendor driver JAR is deployed separately on the classpath or module path and DriverManager discovers implementations of java.sql.Driver through the ServiceLoader mechanism at initialization.

.NET plugin hosts (Microsoft's documented AppWithPlugin design): host and plugins compile against a shared contract assembly only; each implementation assembly is loaded later in a private AssemblyLoadContext via AssemblyDependencyResolver, so plugins ship and version independently of the host and may even carry conflicting dependencies.

Python plugin ecosystems (pytest and its hook plugins, flake8/black plugins): the host declares an entry-point group as the contract and discovers implementations installed as separate distributions through importlib.metadata.entry_points(), never importing a plugin package by name.
avoid_when: One implementation, one consumer and no deployment boundary: the concrete type is simpler and the interface only adds a file to keep in sync.

The language satisfies interfaces structurally and the consumer can declare the contract where it uses it (Go): a separate contract package is optional unless other consumers or a deployment rule need it.
A framework already owns the boundary (DI container registrations of concrete types, message bus, RPC framework); a parallel interface layer duplicates it.
Sealed systems where no second implementation will ever exist and no unit must be deployed without the implementation.
Hot paths where the indirection (virtual dispatch, boxing, dyn, pimpl) is measurable and substitutability is not required.
anti_patterns: Interface-per-class: mirroring every class with a single-implementation interface (the 'IHammer' syndrome) - the contract carries no independent meaning and both must be edited together.
Leaky contract: the interface's signatures name infrastructure types (connections, HTTP requests, ORM entities), so the client ends up depending on the implementation anyway.
Fat contract: one interface per component with dozens of members, forcing every implementation and test fake to implement everything (a violation of interface segregation).
Separation in name only: the interface lives in the implementation's package and the client depends on that package; the dependency arrow is unchanged.
Unversioned published contract: changing a deployed service provider interface without a compatibility strategy, breaking third-party implementors.
Using a service locator as the wiring mechanism while calling it dependency injection, hiding the client's real dependencies.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: both the client and the implementation depend on the abstraction, not on each other.
Acyclic and stable dependencies: the contract unit must not depend on implementation units, and should depend on little else.
Interface segregation: contracts are narrow and shaped by one client's needs, not by an implementation's full surface.
Information hiding: the implementation's types and details stay private to its own unit.
Open/closed principle: new implementations plug in at the composition root without modifying clients.
Separation of concerns: using a dependency and choosing one are different responsibilities owned by different code.
best_practices: Put the contract in its own unit (package/module/crate/assembly/header) with a minimal dependency set, and let both sides depend on it.
Express the contract in domain terms; never let infrastructure types into its signatures.
Wire implementations in a single composition root; clients receive the contract through constructor injection.
Keep contracts small and cohesive; add a new interface rather than widening one that third parties already implement.
Version published contracts deliberately: default methods, optional capabilities, or a new interface for breaking changes.
Test the contract once and run that suite against every implementation; in static languages add a compile-time conformance assertion.
For ABI boundaries choose the mechanism deliberately (header plus opaque handle, pure abstract class, pimpl) and document the compatibility promise.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Separated Interface (Base Patterns chapter): define an interface in a separate package from its implementation.
